questions.q: Simple shear with γ = 0.75. Stretch λ of the fiber initially along e₂ (dimensionless, 3 significant figures)?
questions.x: With N = e₂, λ = √(N·CN) = √C_22 = √(1 + γ²) = √1.5625 = 1.25, while the fiber along e₁ keeps λ = 1.

questions.q: Simple shear with γ = 0.5. Decrease in angle between fibers initially along e₁ and e₂, in degrees (2 decimals)?
questions.x: cos θ = C_12/√(C_11C_22) = γ/√(1 + γ²), so the angle change π/2 − θ equals arctan γ = arctan 0.5 = 26.57°.

questions.q: Nanson's formula: a reference area element N dA maps to the deformed n da as:
questions.a: n da = J F⁻ᵀ N dA
w: n da = J F N dA
n da = J⁻¹ Fᵀ N dA
questions.x: Nanson's formula n da = JF⁻ᵀN dA follows from dv = J dV applied to a cylinder built on the area element, and it underlies P = JσF⁻ᵀ.

questions.q: Small strain theory: the infinitesimal rotation tensor ω is:
questions.x: The displacement gradient splits as ∇u = ε + ω, with ε symmetric (strain) and ω = ½(∇u − ∇uᵀ) skew (local rigid rotation).

questions.q: Complete the 2D compatibility equation
questions.x: Differentiating ε_11 = u_1,1, ε_22 = u_2,2 and 2ε_12 = u_1,2 + u_2,1 gives ε_11,22 + ε_22,11 = 2ε_12,12, the condition for a single valued displacement field.

questions.q: A strain field ε(x) is integrated to find u. What remains undetermined?
w: A uniform dilatation of the whole body
A constant shear strain in each plane
A displacement proportional to the strain
questions.x: Fields with ε = 0 have u = c + ω × x, so integration fixes u up to rigid body terms, which supports or symmetry conditions then set.

questions.q: A 2D strain field ε_11 = ax², ε_22 = 0, ε_12 = 0. Is it compatible?
questions.a: Yes, each term of the equation is zero
w: Only when a = 0, since ε_11,22 is nonzero
Only for ν = 0, since ε_22 is coupled
Only if ε_12 = ax is added to balance
questions.x: ε_11,22 = 0, ε_22,11 = 0 and ε_12,12 = 0, so compatibility holds and u_1 = ax³/3 (plus rigid body terms) produces it.

questions.q: Order the steps to recover u from a given 2D strain field
steps: Integrate ε_11 = u_1,1 for u_1 up to a function f(x₂)
Integrate ε_22 = u_2,2 for u_2 up to a function g(x₁)
Substitute into 2ε_12 = u_1,2 + u_2,1 to find f and g
Fix the rigid body constants from the supports
questions.x: Compatibility guarantees integrability, each normal strain is integrated with an unknown function of the other coordinate, the shear strain fixes those functions, and supports set the rigid body terms.

questions.q: Plane stress σ_x = 50, σ_y = −10, τ_xy = 40 MPa. Normal stress σ_x' on an x' axis rotated 30° counterclockwise from x (MPa, 1 decimal)?
σ = [[60,20,0],[20,30,0],[0,0,10]] MPa. Normal stress on the plane with n = (1,1,1)/√3 (MPa, 1 decimal)?
Octahedral shear stress in terms of principal stresses:
questions.x: τ_oct = (1/3)√(Σ(σᵢ − σⱼ)²) = √(2J₂/3), so τ_oct = (√2/3)σ_vm and octahedral shear yield matches von Mises.

questions.q: Rotating a plane stress element by θ corresponds on Mohr's circle to:
questions.a: A rotation of 2θ around the circle
w: A rotation of θ around the circle
A rotation of θ/2 around the circle
A rotation of 4θ in the opposite sense
questions.x: Transformation formulas depend on 2θ, so the point representing a plane moves 2θ around the circle, and principal planes 90° apart lie at opposite ends of a diameter.

questions.q: In the proof that σ* = QσQᵀ, which observer change facts are used?
questions.a: t* = Qt and n* = Qn for every plane
w: t* = t and n* = Qn for every plane
t* = Qt and n* = n for every plane
t* = QᵀtQ and n* = Qᵀn on each plane
questions.x: Traction and normal are spatial vectors, so σ*Qn = Qσn for every n, which gives σ* = QσQᵀ.

questions.q: Complete the second stress invariant
questions.x: I₂ = ½[(tr σ)² − tr(σ²)] = σ₁σ₂ + σ₂σ₃ + σ₃σ₁, and the characteristic equation is s³ − I₁s² + I₂s − I₃ = 0.

questions.q: A hydrostatic stress σ = −pI is drawn on Mohr's circle. The result is:
questions.a: A single point at −p with zero shear
w: A circle of radius p centered at the origin
A circle of radius p/2 through the origin
questions.x: For σ = −pI every plane carries normal stress −p and zero shear, so every direction is principal and the Mohr circle collapses to a point.

questions.q: Match each Mohr's circle feature (plane stress) to its value
questions.x: The center is the mean in-plane normal stress, the radius equals the maximum in-plane shear, and the circle meets the σ axis at the principal stresses.

questions.q: Complete the inverse isotropic Hooke's law
questions.x: Inverting σ = λ tr(ε)I + 2με gives ε = [(1 + ν)σ − ν tr(σ)I]/E, so ε_11 = [σ_11 − ν(σ_22 + σ_33)]/E.

questions.q: Young's modulus in terms of the Lamé constants λ and μ:
questions.x: E = μ(3λ + 2μ)/(λ + μ) and ν = λ/(2(λ + μ)), while (3λ + 2μ)/3 is the bulk modulus K.

questions.q: Aluminum, E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.30, under hydrostatic pressure 100 MPa. Magnitude of the volumetric strain, in units of 10⁻³ (3 significant figures)?
Principal stresses 100, −100, 0 MPa. von Mises and Tresca equivalent stresses?
questions.x: σ_vm = √(½[200² + 100² + 100²]) = 173 MPa and Tresca σ_max − σ_min = 200 MPa, so Tresca is the more conservative criterion here.

questions.q: Steel bar, L = 1 m, E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K, with a 0.3 mm gap to a rigid wall, is heated 50 K. Magnitude of the compressive stress (MPa)?
questions.x: Free expansion αΔTL = 0.6 mm closes the 0.3 mm gap, so the wall suppresses 0.3 mm and σ = E(0.3/1000) = 60 MPa compression.

questions.q: The deviatoric stress s = σ − (tr σ/3)I has which property?
questions.a: tr s = 0, and it drives shape change
w: det s = 0, and it drives volume change
s = sᵀ only for isotropic solids
tr s = tr σ, and it sets the pressure
questions.x: The deviator has zero trace, s = 2Ge in isotropic elasticity, and its invariant J₂ = ½s:s governs von Mises yielding.

questions.q: A ductile metal (σ_y = 300 MPa) is under 1 GPa hydrostatic pressure. von Mises predicts:
questions.x: Hydrostatic stress has zero deviator, so J₂ = 0 and σ_vm = 0, and the metal deforms elastically with tr ε = −p/K.

questions.q: Match each isotropic constant to its expression
questions.x: With Lamé constants λ and μ: K = λ + 2μ/3, ν = λ/(2(λ + μ)), G = μ and E = 2G(1 + ν).

questions.q: Which polynomial Airy functions satisfy ∇⁴φ = 0 for arbitrary coefficients?
questions.a: All terms of degree 3 and lower
w: All terms of degree 4 and lower
Only the degree 2 and degree 4 terms
questions.x: ∇⁴ takes four derivatives, so cubics and lower vanish identically, and degree 4 and higher terms need coefficient relations.

questions.q: Complete the biharmonic check for φ = Ax⁴ + Bx²y² + Cy⁴
questions.x: ∇⁴φ = φ,xxxx + 2φ,xxyy + φ,yyyy = 24A + 2(4B) + 24C, so biharmonic requires 3A + B + 3C = 0.

questions.q: Why does the uniformly loaded simply supported beam need a fifth degree Airy polynomial?
w: σ_22 ∝ y² needs φ ∝ y⁵ alone
questions.x: The moment varies as x², so bending stress ∝ x²y requires φ ∝ x²y³, and a y⁵ term restores ∇⁴φ = 0.

questions.q: A beam face y = c is traction free. Conditions on the Airy function there:
questions.x: On y = c, n = e₂ gives σ_22 = φ,xx = 0 and σ_12 = −φ,xy = 0.

questions.q: Complete the polar Airy shear stress
questions.x: In polar coordinates σ_rθ = −∂/∂r((1/r)∂φ/∂θ), with σ_θθ = ∂²φ/∂r² and σ_rr = (1/r)φ,r + (1/r²)φ,θθ.

questions.q: Flamant problem: line load P = 10 kN/m normal to a half-plane, σ_rr = −2P cos θ/(πr) with θ from the load line. |σ_rr| at r = 0.1 m, θ = 0 (kPa, 1 decimal)?
questions.x: σ_rr = −2P/(πr) = −2(10)/(π·0.1) = −63.7 kPa directly beneath the load.

questions.q: Kirsch: σ_θθ = (σ₀/2)(1 + a²/r²) − (σ₀/2)(1 + 3a⁴/r⁴)cos 2θ, θ from the load axis, σ₀ = 100 MPa. σ_θθ at r = 2a, θ = 90° (MPa, 1 decimal)?
questions.x: With cos 2θ = −1, σ_θθ = 50(1.25) + 50(1.1875) = 121.9 MPa, down from 300 MPa at the hole edge.

questions.q: In the Flamant solution σ_rr = −2P cos θ/(πr), the stress state is:
w: Hydrostatic, σ_rr = σ_θθ at each point
questions.x: φ = −(P/π) rθ sin θ gives a radial stress field, and contours of constant σ_rr are circles tangent to the surface at the load point.

questions.q: Thick closed-end cylinder, a = 100 mm, b = 200 mm, internal pressure 30 MPa. Axial stress far from the ends (MPa)?
questions.x: End cap balance gives σ_zz = pa²/(b² − a²) = 30(10⁴)/(3 × 10⁴) = 10 MPa, equal to the Lamé constant A.

questions.q: Thin cylinder, p = 1.5 MPa, R = 400 mm, t = 8 mm, with a helical weld at 45° to the axis. Normal stress across the weld (MPa, 2 decimals)?
questions.x: σ_θ = pR/t = 75 MPa and σ_x = 37.5 MPa, so at 45° σ_n = (σ_θ + σ_x)/2 = 56.25 MPa.

questions.q: Thick sphere under pressure: Lamé-type stress solution with constants A and B?
w: σ_rr = A − B/r², σ_θθ = A + B/r²
questions.x: Spherical equilibrium dσ_rr/dr + 2(σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0 with u = Cr + D/r² gives σ_rr = A − 2B/r³ and σ_θθ = A + B/r³.

questions.q: Shrink fitting an outer cylinder onto an inner cylinder is done to:
questions.a: Prestress the bore in hoop compression
w: Raise the hoop stress uniformly in both cylinders
Remove the radial stress at the inner bore
Make the axial stress equal to the hoop stress
questions.x: The interference δ creates an interface pressure that leaves residual hoop compression at the bore, which offsets the tensile hoop stress from internal pressure.

questions.q: Set b = a + t with t/a → 0 in σ_θθ(a) = p(a² + b²)/(b² − a²). The limit is:
questions.x: b² − a² ≈ 2at and a² + b² ≈ 2a², so σ_θθ(a) → pa/t, recovering thin-wall theory.

questions.q: Thin closed-end cylinder (σ₃ ≈ 0), von Mises. Internal pressure at first yield?
questions.x: With σ₁ = pR/t and σ₂ = pR/(2t), σ_vm = (√3/2)pR/t, so yield occurs at p = 2σ_y t/(√3 R).

questions.q: Complete the radial displacement of a thin closed-end cylinder
questions.x: Hoop strain ε_θ = (σ_θ − νσ_x)/E = (pR/(Et))(1 − ν/2), and Δr = Rε_θ.

questions.q: Match each pressure vessel result
pairs: σ_rr + σ_θθ in a Lamé cylinder
questions.x: In a Lamé cylinder σ_rr + σ_θθ = 2A, the closed-end axial stress is uniform and equal to A, the interference fixes the contact pressure, and the sphere hoop stress is A + B/r³.

questions.q: For a hyperelastic material with strain energy W(C), the second Piola stress is:
questions.x: Since E = ½(C − I), S = ∂W/∂E = 2∂W/∂C, and the first Piola stress is P = ∂W/∂F = FS.

questions.q: The incompressible neo-Hookean strain energy is:
questions.x: With I₁ = tr C = λ₁² + λ₂² + λ₃² and J = 1, W = (μ/2)(I₁ − 3), where μ is the small strain shear modulus.

questions.q: Complete the Mooney-Rivlin strain energy
questions.x: Mooney-Rivlin adds the second invariant, W = C₁(I₁ − 3) + C₂(I₂ − 3), with initial shear modulus μ = 2(C₁ + C₂).

questions.q: Incompressible neo-Hookean bar, μ = 0.5 MPa, uniaxial stretch λ = 2. Cauchy stress σ_11 (MPa, 2 decimals)?
Neo-Hookean simple shear by γ: shear stress and first normal stress difference?
questions.x: B = [[1 + γ², γ],[γ, 1]], so σ = −pI + μB gives σ_12 = μγ (linear) and σ_11 − σ_22 = μγ², the Poynting type normal stress effect.

questions.q: Thin neo-Hookean balloon: p = (2μH/R)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷). Hoop stretch λ at the pressure maximum (3 significant figures)?
questions.x: dp/dλ = 0 gives −λ⁻² + 7λ⁻⁸ = 0, so λ⁶ = 7 and λ = 7^(1/6) ≈ 1.38.

questions.q: Pressure-controlled inflation of that balloon past the pressure maximum:
questions.a: Runs away to ever larger radius
w: Deflates back to the reference radius
questions.x: The pressure maximum is a limit point and the neo-Hookean pressure then falls toward zero, so under controlled pressure the radius grows dynamically without bound; strain stiffening models (Mooney-Rivlin, Ogden, Gent) supply a stable state at larger stretch.

questions.q: Order the steps for incompressible neo-Hookean uniaxial tension
steps: Set λ₁ = λ and λ₂ = λ₃ = λ^(−1/2) from J = 1
Write σ = −pI + μB with B = diag(λ², 1/λ, 1/λ)
Use the free lateral face σ_22 = 0 to get p = μ/λ
questions.x: Incompressibility fixes the lateral stretch, the pressure p acts as a Lagrange multiplier set by the traction free faces, and σ_11 follows.

questions.q: Euler-Almansi strain e relates to Green-Lagrange strain E by:
questions.x: Pushing E forward with F⁻ᵀ(·)F⁻¹ gives e = ½(I − B⁻¹), the spatial strain, so ds² − dS² = 2dX·E dX = 2dx·e dx.

questions.q: C = FᵀF and B = FFᵀ share:
questions.a: Eigenvalues λᵢ², eigenvectors related by R
w: The same eigenvalues λᵢ, eigenvectors equal
The same trace only, other invariants differ
questions.x: C = U² lives in the reference configuration and B = V² in the current one, with V = RURᵀ, so their eigenvalues are the squared principal stretches.

questions.q: The first Piola traction PN relates to the Cauchy traction σn by:
questions.a: PN dA = σn da, the same force
w: PN da = σn dA, the same force
PN = J σn on every surface
questions.x: P is defined so the actual force df = σn da equals PN dA, which follows from Nanson's formula n da = JF⁻ᵀN dA.

questions.q: W = (μ/2)(I₁ − 3) − μ ln J + (λ/2)(ln J)². Linearizing about F = I gives:
questions.a: Hooke's law with Lamé λ and μ
w: Hooke's law with shear modulus μ/2
Hooke's law with bulk modulus λ
questions.x: Expanding to second order in ε gives W ≈ μ ε:ε + (λ/2)(tr ε)², which is linear isotropic elasticity with the same λ and μ.

questions.q: Uniaxial stretch λ = 2 (fiber along e₁). Euler-Almansi strain e_11 (3 decimals)?
Small strain Young's modulus of an incompressible neo-Hookean solid:
questions.x: dσ_11/dλ = μ(2λ + 1/λ²) equals 3μ at λ = 1, matching E = 2μ(1 + ν) with ν = 1/2.

questions.q: Complete the push-forward of the second Piola stress
questions.x: σ = J⁻¹FSFᵀ, the inverse of S = JF⁻¹σF⁻ᵀ.

questions.q: Match each finite strain tensor
questions.x: C and E are referential measures, B and e are spatial, and E is work conjugate to the second Piola stress S.

questions.q: The material time derivative of a spatial field φ(x, t) is:
questions.x: Following a particle, Dφ/Dt = ∂φ/∂t + v·∇φ, the local rate plus the convective rate.

questions.q: Spatial velocity v₁ = 2x₁ (m/s) and temperature T = 3x₁ + 5t (K, x₁ in m, t in s). DT/Dt at x₁ = 1 m (K/s)?
The spatial velocity gradient L in terms of F:
questions.x: L = grad v = ḞF⁻¹, and it splits into D = sym L and W = skew L.

questions.q: For a rigid body motion, the rate of deformation D and spin W satisfy:
questions.a: D = 0, and W is the angular velocity tensor
w: W = 0, and D is the angular velocity tensor
D = W, both equal to the angular velocity
D = I, and W is the rotation tensor
questions.x: A rigid motion has v = v₀ + ω × x, so L is skew, D = 0, and W carries the angular velocity.

questions.q: Complete the spatial continuity equation
questions.x: Mass conservation in spatial form is ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρv) = 0, equivalently Dρ/Dt + ρ∇·v = 0.

questions.q: The rate of change of the volume ratio, J̇, equals:
questions.x: J̇ = J tr L = J∇·v, so ρJ = ρ₀ gives ρ̇ = −ρ∇·v, and isochoric motion means ∇·v = 0.

questions.q: Reynolds transport theorem for a material volume Ω(t):
questions.x: Mapping to the reference volume, d/dt ∫φJ dV uses J̇ = J∇·v, giving ∫(Dφ/Dt + φ∇·v) dv = ∫∂φ/∂t dv + ∮φv·n da.

questions.q: Referential (Lagrangian) form of linear momentum balance:
questions.x: Pulling back div σ + b = ρa with Nanson's formula gives Div P + b₀ = ρ₀a, where b₀ = Jb and Div uses X.

questions.q: In referential form, angular momentum balance requires:
w: P = Pᵀ, so S is skew
F P = P F, so σ is skew
questions.x: σ = σᵀ with σ = J⁻¹PFᵀ gives PFᵀ = FPᵀ, so P is generally unsymmetric while S = F⁻¹P is symmetric.

questions.q: Stress power per unit reference volume equals:
questions.x: The work conjugate pairs are (σ, D) per current volume and (P, Ḟ), (S, Ė) per reference volume, all equal to Jσ:D.

questions.q: Velocity v = (4x₂, 0, 0) with v in m/s and x in m. Rate of deformation component D_12 (s⁻¹)?
Uniform density ρ = 1000 kg/m³ with v = α(x₁, x₂, x₃), α = 0.1 s⁻¹. Dρ/Dt (kg/(m³·s))?
questions.x: ∇·v = 3α = 0.3 s⁻¹, so Dρ/Dt = −ρ∇·v = −300 kg/(m³·s), an expanding flow.

questions.q: Complete the local energy balance (q = heat flux, r = heat source)
questions.x: The first law in local form is ρė = σ:D − div q + ρr, with σ:D the stress power.

questions.q: In the principle of virtual work, the virtual displacements δu must:
questions.x: δu is kinematically admissible: δu = 0 on the Dirichlet boundary, and ∫σ:δε dv = ∫b·δu dv + ∫t·δu da holds for all such δu.

questions.q: Order the path from strong form to a finite element system
steps: Strong form: div σ + b = 0 with boundary conditions
Multiply by δu and integrate by parts: weak form
Restrict u and δu to a finite trial space: Ritz/Galerkin
Use piecewise local shape functions: finite elements
Assemble and solve K u = f
questions.x: The weak form lowers the smoothness requirement, Ritz/Galerkin discretizes it, and finite elements use local bases that give a sparse assembled stiffness matrix.

questions.q: Match each description or kinematic rate
pairs: Fields as functions of X and t
Fields as functions of x and t
questions.x: Solid mechanics usually tracks particles by X, fluid mechanics uses fixed points x, and L = D + W splits into stretching and spin.

questions.q: A free isotropic body is uniformly heated by ΔT. Its strain and stress are:
w: ε = αΔT I and σ = −EαΔT I
questions.x: Isotropic thermal strain is a pure dilatation αΔT I, and an unconstrained body with a uniform ΔT expands stress free.

questions.q: Aluminum plate, E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ /K, fully constrained in both in-plane directions, heated 40 K. Magnitude of the in-plane stress (MPa, 1 decimal)?
Complete the stress in a bar with both ends fixed, heated by ΔT
questions.x: Zero total strain gives σ/E + αΔT = 0, so σ = −EαΔT, compressive on heating.

questions.q: A bimetallic strip is heated. It curves so that:
questions.a: The lower α layer is on the concave side
w: The higher α layer is on the concave side
It stays straight and only extends
questions.x: The higher α layer expands more and ends on the convex side, and the curvature scales with (α₂ − α₁)ΔT divided by the thickness.

questions.q: Unidirectional carbon/epoxy, V_f = 0.6, E_f = 230 GPa, E_m = 3.5 GPa. Rule of mixtures E₁ along fibers (GPa, 1 decimal)?
questions.x: Equal strain (Voigt) gives E₁ = V_fE_f + V_mE_m = 138 + 1.4 = 139.4 GPa.

questions.q: Same lamina. Inverse rule of mixtures estimate of transverse E₂ (GPa, 2 decimals)?
questions.x: Equal stress (Reuss) gives 1/E₂ = V_f/E_f + V_m/E_m, so E₂ = 8.55 GPa, a lower bound estimate.

questions.q: The transverse modulus E₂ of a unidirectional lamina is dominated by:
questions.a: The matrix, since the phases act in series
w: The fibers, since the phases act in parallel
The fiber volume fraction alone, linearly
The interface strength of the lamina
questions.x: In the transverse direction fiber and matrix carry the same stress, so the compliant matrix controls E₂ and the inverse rule of mixtures applies.

questions.q: A unidirectional carbon/epoxy lamina is strongest under:
questions.x: Longitudinal tension loads the strong fibers directly, while longitudinal compression is limited by matrix-supported microbuckling and the transverse and shear strengths are matrix dominated and far lower.

questions.q: Longitudinal compressive strength of carbon/epoxy is limited mainly by:
w: Fiber tensile rupture at the surface
questions.x: Thin fibers in compression rely on lateral matrix support, so failure occurs by microbuckling and kink band formation at a fraction of the tensile strength.

questions.q: A chalk stick twisted to failure breaks along a 45° helix because:
questions.a: It fails on the max tensile stress plane
w: It fails on the maximum shear stress plane
It fails where the axial stress peaks
It fails on the octahedral shear plane
questions.x: Torsion gives pure shear with principal tension at 45°, and brittle materials such as chalk and glass fail by maximum principal tensile stress.

questions.q: Complete the orthotropic reciprocity relation
questions.x: A symmetric compliance matrix gives S_12 = −ν₁₂/E₁ = −ν₂₁/E₂, so a stiff fiber direction gives a small ν₂₁.

questions.q: Laminate law [N; M] = [[A, B],[B, D]][ε⁰; κ]. A symmetric layup gives:
questions.a: B = 0, so extension and bending decouple
w: A = 0, so in-plane loads give only bending
D = 0, so bending stiffness comes from A
B = A, so stretching and bending are equal
questions.x: B = ∫Q̄z dz vanishes when plies mirror about the midplane, so in-plane loads produce only midplane strains.

questions.q: An unsymmetric [0/90] laminate is cured hot and cooled. It:
questions.a: Warps, via B coupling to curvature
w: Stays flat, because the A matrix is balanced
Develops stress only in the matrix-rich edges
questions.x: Thermal resultants N_T and M_T act through B ≠ 0, so the cooldown produces curvature, which symmetric layups avoid.

questions.q: Which bounds on effective moduli are tighter than Voigt and Reuss for isotropic two-phase composites?
questions.x: Voigt and Reuss bound K and G from above and below, and Hashin-Shtrikman variational bounds lie between them for macroscopically isotropic composites.

questions.q: Match each layup to its stiffness property
pairs: A_16, A_26, D_16, D_26 all zero
questions.x: Balance removes in-plane shear coupling, the quasi-isotropic layup has isotropic A, symmetric cross-ply has zero coupling terms, and antisymmetric angle-ply couples extension to twist.

questions.q: Order the steps of classical lamination theory
steps: Ply stiffness Q in material axes from E₁, E₂, ν₁₂, G₁₂
Rotate each ply to Q̄ using its angle θ
Integrate A, B, D through the thickness
Invert [[A, B],[B, D]] for ε⁰ and κ under N and M
Recover ply strains and stresses in material axes for failure checks
questions.x: Plane stress ply constants build Q, rotation gives Q̄, thickness integration gives ABD, inversion gives midplane strains and curvatures, and ply stresses follow from ε = ε⁰ + zκ.

boards.prompt: I give you a 2D strain field. How do you know it came from a real displacement field, and how do you get u back? Now what if the domain has a hole?
points: Compatibility ε_11,22 + ε_22,11 = 2ε_12,12 is the integrability condition in 2D
Integrate the normal strains, each giving u up to a function of the other coordinate
The shear strain equation fixes those functions up to rigid body terms
Rigid body terms u = c + ω × x come from supports
For a multiply connected domain, single valued displacement also requires zero dislocation (Cesàro) integrals around each hole

boards.prompt: Take a small square of material with unit normal N on one face. Tell me how its area and normal change, and how the angle between two edges changes.
points: Nanson: n da = JF⁻ᵀN dA
Area ratio da/dA = J√(N·C⁻¹N)
Fiber stretch λ = √(N·CN)
cos θ = N₁·CN₂/(λ₁λ₂) for initially perpendicular N₁ and N₂
In small strain the angle decrease is 2ε_12 for fibers along e₁ and e₂

boards.prompt: Draw Mohr's circle for σ_x = 80, σ_y = −40, τ_xy = 30 MPa. Find the principal stresses and their orientation. Now what is the absolute maximum shear once you include the third direction?
points: Center (σ_x + σ_y)/2 = 20 MPa and radius √(60² + 30²) ≈ 67.1 MPa
σ₁ ≈ 87.1 MPa and σ₂ ≈ −47.1 MPa
tan 2θ_p = 2τ_xy/(σ_x − σ_y) = 0.5, so θ_p ≈ 13.3°
With σ₃ = 0 between σ₁ and σ₂, the absolute maximum shear equals the in-plane value ≈ 67.1 MPa
When σ₁ and σ₂ share a sign, the absolute maximum shear is half the larger principal stress magnitude, acting out of plane

boards.prompt: Prove that the Cauchy stress is objective. Then tell me whether its material time derivative is objective, and what you do about it in a rate law.
points: Under x* = Qx + c, traction and normal transform as t* = Qt and n* = Qn
σ*Qn = Qσn for every n gives σ* = QσQᵀ
Differentiating gives σ̇* = Qσ̇Qᵀ + Q̇σQᵀ + QσQ̇ᵀ, which carries spin terms
Rate laws use objective rates such as the Jaumann rate σ̇ − Wσ + σW
Referential measures S and E are invariant under observer change, which avoids the issue

boards.prompt: A bar sits between two rigid walls and is heated by ΔT. Find the stress. Now leave a small gap δ at one end. What changes?
points: Total strain is mechanical plus thermal, ε = σ/E + αΔT
Rigid walls set ε = 0, so σ = −EαΔT
With a gap, the bar expands freely until αΔTL = δ
Beyond that, σ = −E(αΔT − δ/L)
The stress is independent of the bar length for full constraint

boards.prompt: Compare Tresca and von Mises. Draw both in the σ₁, σ₂ plane for plane stress and tell me where they differ most.
points: Tresca uses maximum shear (σ_max − σ_min)/2 = σ_y/2
von Mises uses J₂: σ_vm = √(3J₂) = σ_y
In the principal stress plane Tresca is a hexagon inscribed in the von Mises ellipse
They agree in uniaxial and equibiaxial tension
They differ most in pure shear: Tresca τ_y = σ_y/2 and von Mises τ_y = σ_y/√3 ≈ 0.577σ_y

boards.prompt: Simply supported beam, length 2L, depth 2c, uniform load q on the top face. Set up the Airy stress function solution.
points: Choose a polynomial up to fifth degree, including x²y³ and a y⁵ correction
Impose ∇⁴φ = 0 to relate the fifth degree coefficients
Top face: σ_22 = −q and σ_12 = 0 at y = c, bottom face traction free at y = −c
Ends: zero axial force and moment, shear resultant qL, applied in Saint-Venant sense
Result: σ_11 equals the beam theory My/I plus a correction of order q, and σ_22 varies cubically through the depth

boards.prompt: A point load presses on a half-space. Give me the Flamant solution. Now what happens as r → 0, and how would you handle a distributed pressure?
points: φ = −(P/π) rθ sin θ gives σ_rr = −2P cos θ/(πr) and σ_θθ = σ_rθ = 0
Force balance on a semicircle of radius r reproduces P
The stress is singular as 1/r at the load point, where plasticity or contact spreads the load
Circles of constant σ_rr pass through the load point
A distributed pressure follows by superposition, integrating the Flamant kernel over the loaded strip

boards.prompt: Two thick cylinders are shrink fitted with radial interference δ. How do you find the interface pressure and the final stresses under internal pressure?
points: Unknown interface pressure p_c acts outward on the outer cylinder and inward on the inner one
Each cylinder takes the Lamé solution with its own A and B
Compatibility: u_outer(c) − u_inner(c) = δ at the interface radius c
This gives p_c, and the residual stresses add to the operating stresses by superposition
The bore ends with lower peak hoop stress, which raises the allowable pressure

boards.prompt: Thick cylinder, internal pressure, Tresca yield. Can I raise the burst pressure indefinitely by making the wall thicker? Now what about a sphere?
points: Maximum shear at the bore is (σ_θθ − σ_rr)/2 = pb²/(b² − a²)
As b → ∞ this tends to p, so first yield occurs at p = σ_y/2 at most
Extra thickness gives diminishing return, and autofrettage or shrink fits raise capacity
A thick sphere has σ_rr = A − 2B/r³ and σ_θθ = A + B/r³
The sphere bore shear is 3pb³/(4(b³ − a³)), tending to 3p/4

boards.prompt: Take an incompressible neo-Hookean bar in uniaxial tension. Derive the stress-stretch relation and compare it with linear elasticity.
points: J = 1 gives λ₂ = λ₃ = λ^(−1/2)
σ = −pI + μB, with p a Lagrange multiplier for incompressibility
Free lateral faces give p = μ/λ, so σ_11 = μ(λ² − 1/λ)
Nominal stress P_11 = σ_11/λ = μ(λ − 1/λ²)
Near λ = 1 the slope is 3μ = E, the linear result with ν = 1/2

boards.prompt: You blow up a spherical rubber balloon. Sketch pressure against stretch. Why is it hard to start inflating, and what happens at the peak?
points: Membrane balance p = 2σH/(λ³R), using r = λR and thickness h = H/λ²
Neo-Hookean gives p = (2μH/R)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷)
The pressure peaks at λ = 7^(1/6) ≈ 1.38
The peak is a limit point, so under pressure control the radius runs away, arrested only by strain stiffening
Volume control traces the full curve, and strain stiffening models (Mooney-Rivlin, Ogden) give a later rise

boards.prompt: Shear a rubber block in simple shear. What stresses do you need, and how does that differ from linear elasticity?
points: Neo-Hookean gives σ_12 = μγ, linear in γ
Normal stress difference σ_11 − σ_22 = μγ² appears at second order (Poynting effect)
Holding the block in simple shear requires normal tractions on the faces
Linear elasticity captures only the first order shear part

boards.prompt: Tell me what makes a material hyperelastic, how you get stress from W, and how frame indifference restricts W.
points: A strain energy W(F) exists with P = ∂W/∂F, so work is path independent
Frame indifference requires W(QF) = W(F), satisfied by writing W(C)
S = 2∂W/∂C and σ = J⁻¹FSFᵀ
Isotropy makes W a function of the invariants I₁, I₂, J
Incompressibility adds a reaction −pI to σ (−pC⁻¹ to S), with p a Lagrange multiplier

boards.prompt: Derive the continuity equation from conservation of mass, first in referential form and then in spatial form.
points: Mass of a material volume is constant: ∫ρ dv = ∫ρ₀ dV
dv = J dV gives ρJ = ρ₀ pointwise
Differentiating with J̇ = J∇·v gives Dρ/Dt + ρ∇·v = 0
Expanding Dρ/Dt gives ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρv) = 0
Incompressible motion has J = 1 and ∇·v = 0

boards.prompt: Start from the integral balance of linear momentum and get to the local equation. Then use angular momentum to say something about σ.
points: d/dt ∫ρv dv = ∫b dv + ∮t da for every material volume
Reynolds transport with mass conservation gives d/dt ∫ρv dv = ∫ρa dv
Cauchy t = σn and the divergence theorem give ∫(div σ + b − ρa) dv = 0
Arbitrary volume gives div σ + b = ρa pointwise
Angular momentum with zero body couples gives σ = σᵀ

boards.prompt: Contrast the Lagrangian and Eulerian descriptions. Write the acceleration in each, and tell me which one you use for a solid and which for a fluid.
points: Lagrangian fields depend on X and t, Eulerian fields on x and t
Lagrangian acceleration a = ∂²χ/∂t² at fixed X
Eulerian acceleration a = ∂v/∂t + (grad v)v, including the convective term
Solids use the Lagrangian view because the reference shape and boundaries are known
Fluids use the Eulerian view because particles travel far from their start

boards.prompt: Take linear elastostatics. Go from the strong form to the weak form, then to Rayleigh-Ritz and finite elements. What does each step buy you?
points: Strong form: div σ + b = 0 in Ω with u = ū on S_u and σn = t̄ on S_t
Weak form: ∫σ:δε dv = ∫b·δu dv + ∫t̄·δu da for all δu vanishing on S_u
Integration by parts lowers the smoothness needed and makes traction conditions natural
Ritz restricts to a finite trial space, giving an upper bound on stiffness for displacement methods
Finite elements use local piecewise shape functions, giving sparse K and systematic convergence under refinement

boards.prompt: A bar is fixed between rigid walls and heated. Find the stress. Now make it a thin plate constrained on all four edges. Why does the answer change?
points: Bar: ε = σ/E + αΔT = 0 gives σ = −EαΔT
Plate: ε_11 = ε_22 = 0 with σ_33 = 0
Biaxial constraint gives σ_11 = σ_22 = −EαΔT/(1 − ν)
Poisson contraction from the other direction adds to the constraint, raising the stress by 1/(1 − ν)
Full 3D constraint gives σ = −EαΔT/(1 − 2ν) = −3KαΔT

boards.prompt: Estimate the stiffness of a unidirectional fiber composite along and across the fibers. Which estimate do you trust more and why?
points: Along fibers, equal strain gives E₁ = V_fE_f + V_mE_m (Voigt)
Across fibers, equal stress gives 1/E₂ = V_f/E_f + V_m/E_m (Reuss)
E₁ from the rule of mixtures is accurate because the equal strain assumption holds closely
E₂ from Reuss underestimates, and Halpin-Tsai or Hashin-Shtrikman give better transverse values
Voigt and Reuss bound the true modulus from above and below

boards.prompt: Write the ABD relation for a laminate. What does a symmetric layup buy you, what does balance buy you, and what happens to an unsymmetric laminate after cure?
points: N = Aε⁰ + Bκ and M = Bε⁰ + Dκ
A, B, D are integrals of Q̄ times 1, z and z² through the thickness
Symmetric layup gives B = 0, decoupling extension and bending
Balanced layup gives A_16 = A_26 = 0, decoupling in-plane extension and shear
Unsymmetric laminates warp on cooldown because thermal resultants act through B

boards.prompt: Compare how carbon fiber composites, glass and chalk fail. Then twist a stick of chalk: where does it break and why?
points: Carbon/epoxy is strongest in fiber tension and weaker in fiber compression (microbuckling)
Transverse and shear strengths are matrix dominated and much lower
Glass and chalk are brittle and fail by maximum principal tensile stress
Torsion is pure shear with principal tension at 45° to the axis
Chalk breaks along a 45° helix perpendicular to the principal tension
